title: Encryption & Secrets
summary: Protecting data on the wire, on disk, and the keys and passwords your services use.

goals.text: Encryption inside the data center and at rest

steps.title: Plain HTTP on café Wi-Fi
body: Alice logs in from a café. The site uses plain http://, so her password and session cookie travel as readable text through the Wi-Fi router and a dozen networks beyond it.
Mallory, on the same Wi-Fi, records the traffic and reads everything — and could even change pages on the way back.

callout.text: Anyone on the path — Wi-Fi, ISP, a compromised router — can read and alter unencrypted traffic.

steps.title: TLS: encrypt the wire
body: With HTTPS, TLS encrypts everything between Alice’s browser and the site. During the handshake the server presents a certificate, signed by a certificate authority the browser trusts, proving it really is shop.example.
Mallory still copies every packet — but sees only random-looking bytes, and can’t alter them without detection.

callout.text: Certificates are free and automatic with Let’s Encrypt. Add HSTS so browsers never fall back to http://.

changes: + TLS certificate on the load balancer

card.title: The TLS handshake
lines: both agree on fresh session keys

steps.title: Case: the certificate expired at 3 a.m.
body: Certificates have an expiry date. This one was renewed by hand once a year — by someone who has since left. At 03:00 it expires, every browser shows a full-page security warning, and most users leave.
An outage caused by a date. Fix: automatic renewal with ACME (Let’s Encrypt, or your cloud’s certificate manager), and an alert 30 days before any certificate expires.

callout.text: Short-lived certificates (90 days or less) force automation — and limit the damage if a private key ever leaks.

card.title: Never expire by surprise
lines: ! renewed by hand, once a year
# check every endpoint, not just www

steps.title: Encrypt inside the data center too
body: The load balancer terminates TLS — and traditionally sent plain traffic onward, trusting the internal network. But one compromised machine inside could then read everything.
Modern systems assume no network is trusted (zero trust): services talk over mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates, so every hop is encrypted and every caller is identified.

callout.text: A service mesh can add mTLS between all services automatically, with short-lived certificates it rotates for you.

changes: ~ LB → app → DB over mutual TLS
+ Every service has its own certificate

steps.title: The stolen backup
body: Every byte on the wire is now safe. Then a database backup is left in a storage bucket that was accidentally made public, and someone copies it.
Encryption in transit does nothing here: the data on disk — every customer’s name, address and order history — is readable.

callout.text: Disks get lost, snapshots get shared, buckets get misconfigured. Data at rest needs its own protection.

steps.title: Encrypt at rest, keep keys elsewhere
body: Encrypt disks, database files and backups. The trick is the key: if it sits next to the data, a thief takes both. So keys live in a separate key management service (KMS), which never hands out its master key.
With envelope encryption, data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is itself encrypted by the KMS. Every use of a key is logged, and access can be revoked.

callout.text: Cloud databases and storage encrypt at rest with a checkbox. For very sensitive fields, also encrypt in the application.

card.title: Envelope encryption
lines: data key —encrypted by→ KMS master key
= steal the disk: no usable key

steps.title: Rotating keys without re-encrypting everything
body: Keys should change regularly — and immediately if one might have leaked. Re-encrypting terabytes of data would take days.
Envelope encryption makes it cheap: create a new master key in the KMS and re-wrap each small data key with it. The data itself is never touched, and new writes simply get fresh data keys.

callout.text: Most KMSs rotate master keys automatically every year and keep old versions to unwrap older data keys.

changes: + Master key v2 in the KMS

card.title: Rotating keys
lines: new master key v2 in the KMS
# new writes use fresh data keys

steps.title: Case: a secret in the code
body: A developer hard-codes the payment provider’s API key in the source to test something, and the repository is public. Bots scan public repositories continuously: the key is found and used within minutes.
Deleting the line doesn’t help — it’s in the git history forever. The only fix is to revoke the key and issue a new one.

callout.text: Secrets in code end up in repos, builds, logs and laptops. Treat any secret that touched git as compromised.

changes: + API key committed to a public repo
− Found by a scanner bot in minutes

steps.title: A secrets manager
body: Keep secrets out of code entirely. The app fetches them at startup from a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), proving its own identity to get only the secrets it needs.
Secrets are rotated regularly — or issued short-lived on demand — and scanners in CI block any commit that looks like a key.

callout.text: Never log secrets, and keep them out of error messages and environment dumps.

changes: + Automatic rotation · secret scanning in CI

steps.title: Case: card numbers — tokenize them
body: Card numbers are the most valuable data you could hold, and every system that stores or even sees them must meet strict rules (PCI DSS). Encrypting them still leaves you holding them.

Better: don’t hold them. The checkout sends the card to a payment provider, which stores it and returns a token like tok_4f2c. Your database, logs and analytics only ever see tokens — worthless to a thief.

callout.text: The safest sensitive data is data you never store. Ask whether you need it at all before deciding how to protect it.

changes: + Payment provider holds the real card numbers

steps.title: End-to-end: even the server can’t read it
body: For private messages you can go further. With end-to-end encryption, Alice’s phone encrypts each message with Bob’s public key; only Bob’s phone holds the private key to decrypt it.
The chat server stores and forwards ciphertext. A breach of the server — or a request to hand over messages — reveals nothing readable.
That’s the idea in one line. Real protocols use the key pairs to agree on a fresh secret key for every message, so a key stolen later can’t unlock old conversations (forward secrecy).

callout.text: The trade-off: the server can’t search, filter or back up readable messages, and losing your device can mean losing history. Signal and WhatsApp use the Signal protocol.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• TLS everywhere outside; mTLS between services inside.
  • Encrypt at rest, with keys held separately in a KMS.
  • Automate certificate renewal; rotate keys by re-wrapping data keys.
  • Keep secrets in a secrets manager, rotate them, scan for leaks.
  • Tokenize what you’d rather not hold at all, like card numbers.
  • End-to-end encryption when even the server shouldn’t read the data.

callout.text: That completes Security. Next module: Shipping — testing changes and getting them to production safely.
